case_name: Jones v. Industrial Wood and Allied Workers of Canada (Local 1-3567)
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Jones v. Industrial Wood and Allied
Workers of Canada (Local 1-3567),

2011 BCSC 926

Date: 20110711

Docket:
S084716

Registry: Vancouver

In
the Matter of the
Labour Relations Code
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 244 and

In
the Matter of Decisions made by the Labour Relations Board of British Columbia

dated January 24, 2008 (BCLRB No. B7/2008) and May 1, 2008 (BCLRB
No. B61/2008) and In the Matter of the
Judicial Review Procedures Act
,

R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 241
, as amended, and In the Matter of the
Administrative
Tribunals Act
,

S.B.C. 2004, c. 45

Between:

Remond
Jones

Petitioner

And

Industrial
Wood and Allied Workers of Canada, Local No. 1-3567;

United Steelworkers of America, Local 1-3567;

Canadian Forest Products Ltd./Produits Forestiers Canadien Pacifique Limitée;
and British Columbia Labour Relations Board

Respondents

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Maisonville

Ruling on Application to Strike Pleadings

Counsel for the Petitioner:

D.
Davison

Counsel for the Industrial Wood &
Allied Workers of Canada and United Steel Workers of America, Local 1-3567:

S.
Anderson

A. Tremblay

Counsel for the Canadian Forest Products
Ltd.:

C.
Jones

Counsel for the British Columbia Labour
Relations Board:

E.
Miller

Place and Dates of Trial/Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

June
22-24, 2010 and

February 14-15, 2011

Place and Date of Ruling:

Vancouver,
B.C.

July
11, 2011

1.  INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

Remond Jones, the petitioner, seeks judicial
review of the decision (“the Original Decision”) of the Labour Relations Board
(the “LRB”) dismissing his complaint under
s. 12
of the
Labour Relations
Code
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 244 (the “
Code
”), and the subsequent
reconsideration and confirmation of that decision under
s. 141
of the
Code

by a panel (the “Reconsideration”). The complaint was made against the
Industrial Wood and Allied Workers of Canada, Local No. 1-3567 and the United
Steel, Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial and
Service Workers International Union Local 1-3567 (the “Union”), with respect to
their alleged failure to represent him fairly in dealings with his employer
Canadian Forest Products Ltd./Produits Forestiers Canadien Pacifique Limitée
(“Canfor” or the “Employer”).

2.  NATURE OF
APPLICATION — STRIKE PLEADINGS AND AFFIDAVIT

[
2
]

At the outset of the hearing, which commenced
June 22, 2010, and completed February 15, 2011, the Union brought an
application to strike certain paragraphs from the petition, and from the
affidavit of the petitioner, which was attached to the affidavit of Hasti
Vahidi.

[
3
]

As the petition for judicial review was filed in
2008, this application is brought under Rule 19(24) of the
Rules of Court
,

B.C. Reg. 221/90
.

3.  POSITION OF THE
UNION

[
4
]

The Union argues that paras. 59, 60, and 62
(incorrectly numbered “53” in the petition) of the petition and paras. 26-30 of
the petitioner’s affidavit be struck on the grounds that they disclose no
reasonable claim, or that they are unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious.

[
5
]

The Union further argues that paras. 19, 21, 23,
24, and 31-33 of the petitioner’s affidavit be struck on the ground that they
contain argument and not facts.

[
6
]

The LRB takes no position on this application.
Canfor similarly takes no position on this application.

4.  IMPUGNED
PARAGRAPHS

[
7
]

The impugned paragraphs of the petition are as
follows:

59.   These events have had a serious and negative impact on the
Petitioner. The events have caused the Petitioner significant stress, anxiety
and physical and mental impairment. The Letter and the Email constitute serious
defamation of the Petitioner. It had detrimentally affected the Petitioner'
work environment, including his position as shop steward. The Petitioner has
suffered and continues to suffer as a result of the conduct of Canfor, the IWA
and the LRB. The Petitioner is forced to seek further employment but is
concerned with the repercussions of the Coburn Report and the comments of his
supervisors and peers as they relate to these incidents. Neither Canfor nor the
IWA could ensure the confidentiality of the documents to the two people listed.

60.   Both Canfor and the IWA were fully aware of the consequences
of their actions. The refusal by Canfor to comply with the Petitioner’s request
to remove and destroy the Letter, the Email and related materials including the
Coburn Report were intended,
inter alia
, to punish the Petitioner for
acting in his capacity as a shop steward with respect to the favoritism, shown
by Canfor to Mulder...

53.

[sic
should be 62] The failure of the IWA to represent the Petitioner is consistent
with the misconduct on the part of senior IWA officials which are detailed in
the August 2005 Commission Report of Local 1-3567, District 3 Administership of
the United Steel, Paper, and Forestry, Rubber Manufacturing, Energy Allied
Industrial and Service Workers, the successor to the IWA.

[
8
]

It is important to note that where Mr. Jones
refers to the “Original Decision” or the “Reconsideration” decision in his
affidavit, he is referring to the decisions that were remitted to the LRB by
Madam Justice Gill, not the decisions before me in the present judicial review.
The impugned paragraphs of the affidavit state as follows:

19.   ln BCLRB No. B216/2005, dated August 22, 2005 Michael Fleming,
Associate Chair of the LRB, issued a decision dismissing the Application for
Reconsideration (the “Reconsideration Decision”). Now shown to me and marked
Exhibit
“L”
to this my affidavit is a true copy of the Reconsideration Decision.
The Reconsideration Panel found, incorrectly, among other things, that I did
not take issue with the facts underlying the Original Panel’s including the
conclusions set out in paragraph 27. Those conclusions were specifically taken
issue with and would have been more fully developed if there had been an oral
hearing and if there had been full disclosure prior to rendering a decision in
this matter...

21.   The Complaint and the various submissions filed on my behalf
set out the key facts that support the Complaint. There were significant issues
regarding the bona fides of the IWA’s investigations and the bona fides of the
actions taken by Canfor with respect to the Katherine Coburn investigation, the
March 18, 2003 Letter and an April 29, 2003 E-mail. In many instances in both
the Original Decision and the Reconsideration Decision, the LRB drew
conclusions that were incorrect, illogical, unreasonable, and unsupported by
the evidence, contrary to the evidence and were untested by cross-examination...

23.   The LRB stated in its Original Decision that it would rely on
my submissions and documents to determine any and all facts including those in
dispute. It clearly did not do that. Further the LRB found in its Original
Decision that:

...the circumstances of Jones (sic) case,
although not visited with disciplinary consequences (see analysis below) fall
in the realm of serious employment transgressions. It is no small matter for an
Employer to conclude that an employee has engaged in sexual harassment.
However, I note that the Employer did not label Jones “a pervert”, “a sexual
deviant” or a “predator” as Jones’ counsel suggests”. (At pages 6 and 7)

I am very troubled by these public findings that have been made
without the opportunity for me to defend myself from such conclusions that are
fundamentally false. The conclusions reached in the absence of an oral hearing
are incorrect, irrational, unreasonable, unfair and contrary to the evidence
purportedly relied upon by the LRB in the absence of an oral hearing. They
confirm that the allegations and the continued existence of the Letter, the
Email and the related documents will have a negative effect on me in the
future.

24.   In the Original and the Reconsideration Decisions, the LRB
made numerous errors of fact. Some of the true facts supported by the material
filed with the LRB include the following:

(a)   Photograph #1 did not contain
any

sexual content;

(b)   None of the
employees in the bargaining unit, including the sole female employee, found
Photograph #2 to be sexually harassing;

(c)   The two
photographs were not directed towards Michael Mulder (“Mulder”);

(d)   Mulder initially
alleged that the photographs were “harassing”, not “sexually harassing”;

(e)   The March 18,
2003 Letter, the April 29
th
2003 Email and the related documents
constituted discipline under Canfor’s Policy and could as well be used against
me in a non-disciplinary manner such as consideration for promotions etc;

(f)    The March 18,
2003 Letter, the April 29
th
2003 Email and related documents contain
findings of inappropriate conduct including sexual harassment that are untrue,
are defamatory and attack me in my capacity as an employee and as a shop
steward;

(g)   The April 29,
2003 E-mail and the May 6
th
2003 letter from Patricia Janzen counsel
for Canfor which presumably also remains as part of my record, refers to both
photographs as constituting sexual harassment, which is not possible as
Photograph #1 has no sexual content among other reasons and the Email
fundamentally altered the March 18, 2003 letter by making it more disciplinary
in nature. Ms. Janzen’s claims and assurances which are the basis upon which
the LRB dismissed my Complaint are based on knowledge of the documents and
circumstances pertaining to the investigation and report of Katherine Coburn
and the existence of qualified privilege none of which have been tested by
examination or cross-examination nor have they been supported the documents
related thereto which have not been disclosed to date;

(h)   The IWA’s
statement that it considered the response of Canfor to be “non-disciplinary” is
wrong, as the Letter, the offensive E-mail, investigation report and other
related documents remain in existence. They remain in one of my files and
Canfor has specifically stated that they were being kept because they might
have to be used by Canfor against me in the future;

(I)    The IWA neither
sought nor reviewed the Coburn Report or other related documents nor did they
challenge any of the statements made in the Letter, the Email or the May 6
th

2003 letter of Patricia Janzen;

(j)    In advising
that the IWA would not pursue my grievance to arbitration, Mr. Veale stated
that, in these circumstances, the IWA would assist me in pursuing a
section 12

complaint which they have not done;

(k)   At no time did
the IWA provide assistance to me, either in my capacity as shop steward or as
an employee of Canfor in defending myself in the investigation, pursuing the
grievance on my behalf or in pursuing any
section 12
application;

(I)    Although Mulder
stated that he had never been paid for time he had not worked, Canfor
subsequently admitted that he received preferential treatment for over a year
and cited 50 instances where he had been paid overtime that he was not entitled
to;

(m)  The IWA has not
pursued the grievance with respect to Mulder’s overpayment and that grievance
remains at stage 4 without any further prospects of resolution. That grievance
affects all employees of Canfor and resulted from my investigations and
reporting as a shop steward.

(n)   The IWA did not
conduct a proper investigation of my Grievance. The subsequent events disclosed
in the Steelworkers Report of August 26
th
2005 suggest that the
motivation for not pursuing my legitimate grievance to arbitration was for
improper reasons not for bona fide reasons as concluded by the LRB...

26.   The local executive of the IWA was suspended by the
Steelworkers following audits conducted in 2005 and the filing of harassment
and sexual harassment complaints.

27.   Additionally an investigation and hearing was undertaken by
the Steelworkers with respect to misconduct by IWA officials throughout the
material periods. The Steelworkers provided a report to all members, including
myself, dated August 26th, 2005. Now shown to me and marked
Exhibit “O”

to this my affidavit is a true copy of the report dated August 26, 2005. That
report found that, among other things, certain IWA officials had improperly
spent large amounts of money on inappropriate expenses. The report concluded
that certain officials had misappropriated funds thereby depleting the
financial resources to be used for pursuing grievances, conducting arbitrations
and other matters pertaining to the representation of employees and shop
stewards such as myself. The report found that certain executives of the IWA,
including Sonny Ghag, had engaged in inappropriate conduct and misconduct
including misuse of IWA funds and serious instances of harassment of female IWA
officials. The report recounts evidence of significant sexual harassment by
Sonny Ghag and the use of Union funds to settle sexual harassment claims
without justification and without authority. The report also found that Ghag
harassed and threatened Union officials who disagreed with him or refused to
follow his unlawful or inappropriate directions to union officials. The report
concluded that the environment of the Local Union workplace was one of fear and
intimidation and intolerable behaviour including harassment and sexual
harassment. The report concluded among other things that Sonny Ghag did harass
female employees and members of the Local and was also guilty of financial
misconduct. Mr. Ghag was immediately barred from membership for at least 5
years. The investigation by the Steelworkers continues into the affairs of the Local
and the conduct of union officials including a recommendation that a full audit
going 3 years back be conducted.

28.   The report discloses that the IWA Executive had total
disregard for the rights of members, engaged in harassment and of Union members
and others who challenged the Executive and spent exorbitant amounts of money
on improper purposes. The IWA had a complete disregard for the prohibition and
elimination of harassment, including sexual harassment.

29.   Pictures of a sexual nature remain posted in the Canfor
operation. In fact, contrary to the Original Decision, neither Canfor nor the
IWA has made a concerted effort to create a sexual harassment-free environment.
Now shown to me and marked
Exhibit “P”
to this my affidavit is a true
copy of pictures that were posted by management that are of a sexual-nature.
Three of these photos were in a locked display case to which only management
has keys. This information was included in my submission to the LRB, which was
generally ignored.

Impact of the investigation, the Letter,
the April 29
th
2003 Email and the failure of the Union to pursue the
Grievance

30.   Mulder’s complaint, the subsequent investigation of that
complaint by Katherine Coburn, the letter of March 18, 2003, the subsequent
April 29, 2003 e-mail and the refusal and failure of the Union to properly
represent me, both in my capacity as shop steward and employee, has caused my
family and me significant emotional stress and anxiety. I am currently under
medical care.

31.   The actions taken by Canfor have undermined my position in the
workplace, including my position as shop steward. As found by the Original
Panel, allegations of sexual harassment are significant, serious employment
misconduct. My reputation has been severely damaged.

32.   I am being deeply affected by these proceedings and these
events and it is having a very negative effect on my work environment and my
role as shop steward. I truly believe that I am not guilty of such misconduct
and have not had an opportunity to challenge those findings which remain as
part of my record with Canfor.

33.   Despite the
IWA’s promise to assist me in the section 12 Complaint, the IWA has not done so
and has specifically engaged counsel to fight my Complaint and otherwise act
against my interests. I have incurred significant legal fees and costs to date
that should have been either avoided or paid by the IWA if it had properly
represented me both in my capacity as a shop steward and as an employee under
the Collective Agreement.

5.  JURISPRUDENCE

[
9
]

As noted, this application is brought under Rule 19(24),
in force at the time this matter was initially filed, which states as follows:

At any stage of a proceeding the court may
order to be struck out or amended the whole or any part of an endorsement,
pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a) it
discloses no reasonable claim or defence as the case may be,

(b) it is
unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or vexatious,

(c) it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing or the proceeding, or

(d) it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may grant judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and may
order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
10
]

The Union takes the position that the affidavit
of Mr. Jones was not part of the record because it was filed in support of the
prior application for judicial review to the Supreme Court of British Columbia,
the result of which was that Madam Justice Gill remitted the matter back to the
LRB (
2007 BCSC 673
). However, I understand from Counsel that some of the
material from that judicial review, including the petitioner’s affidavit, was
before Vice-Chair Saunders, having been submitted by Mr. Jones through his then
counsel as an attachment to a submission. The submission was in response to the
request of Vice-Chair Saunders for submissions from the parties on how the
matter should be dealt with from a procedural standpoint in the second hearing.
The Union says it was inappropriate for the affidavit to be submitted in this
manner. No application to adduce fresh evidence had been heard and the matter
was in fact decided on the original complaint and submissions made by the
parties.

[
11
]

All counsel agree that the complete affidavit
with the attached exhibits was before the LRB Reconsideration Panel.

[
12
]

It is certain that the commission report was not
before the Vice-Chair. In any event, the Union now argues that certain portions
of the affidavit should be struck.

[
13
]

In
Creber v. Franklin
,
[1993] B.C.J. No.
890 (S.C.)
, Mr. Justice Spencer noted the irrelevance of adjectives relating to
acts of the other side. Spencer J. held at paragraph 19:

[19]      There
are unsworn letters attached to the affidavits that express the opinions of
their authors. Save where they may be admissible as expert opinions they are
inadmissible. There are adjectival descriptions by one side of the alleged acts
or statements of the other. They are irrelevant. The affidavits should state
the facts only, without stooping to add the deponents descriptive opinion of
those facts. It should be left to argument to persuade the trier of fact what
view he or she should take of them. For counsel to permit affidavits to be
larded with adjectives expressing an opinion about the conduct of the other
side contributes nothing to the fact finding process. On the contrary, it does
a disservice. It exacerbates existing ill feeling, it pads the file with
unnecessary material and it wastes the court's time.

Creber

has been followed on numerous occasions, including in
Kennedy v. Kennedy
,

2006 BCSC 190
.

[
14
]

At para. 5 in
Kennedy
, Ross J. noted the helpful
summary by Master Baker of the decisions in this area:

[5]     In
C.
(K.L.) v. C. (J.)
(2000), 9 R.F.L. (5th) 279,
2000 BCSC 798
, Master Baker
provided a useful summary of the jurisprudence on objectionable affidavits as
follow at para. 9:

Counsel for Mr. C. relies upon
Foote v.
Foote
(1986),
1986 CanLII 986 (BC SC)
, 6 B.C.L.R. (2d) 237 (B.C.S.C.);
Creber v. Franklin
(August
25, 1993), Doc. Vancouver D083222 (B.C.S.C.); and
Webber v. Wallace
, [
[1994]
B.C.J. No. 1894
(August 23, 1994), (B.C.S.C.)].  All are decisions of our
court.  Shortly stated, in all these cases the court directed that
portions of affidavits be expunged for various reasons.  These reasons
include:  hearsay upon hearsay, or irrelevance (
Foote v. Foote
),
inadmissible opinion, adjectival descriptions, or subjective descriptions of
reactions (
Creber
), unidentified witnesses, opinions regarding motives,
or argument (
Webber
).

[
15
]

In
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v.
Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.), Romilly J.
considered when pleadings may be considered “unnecessary,” “scandalous,”
“frivolous,” or “embarrassing”. The test under Rule 19(24) was examined
and it was explained that irrelevant and embarrassing pleadings can be struck
where they do not advance the pleadings and are superfluous and collateral to
the main issues. Romilly J. continued to set out certain principles that can be
distilled from the authorities:

47

Irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded: Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc. (1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
"embarrassing" and "scandalous" pleading is one that is so
irrelevant that it will involve the parties in useless expense and will
prejudice the trial of the action by involving them in a dispute apart from the
issues: Keddie v. Dumas Hotels Ltd. (1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.).
An allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the
proceedings. It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College of Dental Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland (1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499 (B.C.C.A.).
A pleading is "unnecessary" or "vexatious" if it does not
go to establishing the plaintiff's cause of action or does not advance any
claim known in law: Strauts v. Harrigan,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86 (Q.L.)
(B.C.S.C.). A pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out if it is not
necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable: Lutz v. Canadian Puget
Sound Lumber and Timber Co.
(1920), 28 B.C.R 39 (C.A.)
. A pleading is
"frivolous" if it is obviously unsustainable, not in the sense that it
lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of estoppel: Chrisgian
v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 1567
, (6 July 1992), Prince George
Registry 20714 (B.C.S.C.).

The Rule is not limited to pleadings,
but applies equally to other documents, including affidavits.

[
16
]

Additionally, Rule 51(10) also applies to
affidavit evidence. It states:

An affidavit may state only what a deponent
would be permitted to state in evidence at a trial, except that, if the source
of the information is given, an affidavit may contain statements as to the deponent’s
information and belief, if it is made

(a) in respect
of an application for an interlocutory order, or

(b) by leave of the court under
Rule 40 (52) (a) or 52 (8) (e).

[
17
]

Submitting argument in the guise of an affidavit
is improper, as found by Saunders J., as she then was, in
Chamberlain v.
Surrey School District No. 36
,
1998 CanLII 6723 (BC SC)
, [1998] B.C.J. No. 2923 (S.C.) at para.

28
. See also:
The

Sovereign General Insurance Company v. McNeill
,

2007 BCSC 988
.

[
18
]

In a judicial review proceeding, the materials
are generally restricted to the record before the tribunal. Evidence that goes
to the procedural fairness of the decision under review may, in certain
instances, be admissible. For example, while affidavit evidence that a tribunal
made factual findings that are not supported on the record may be admissible in
rare circumstances, it must not amount to a reinterpretation of the record or a
rehearing on the merits:
Kinexus Bioinformatics Corporation v. Asad
,

2010 BCSC 33
at paras.
16-17
.

6.  ISSUE

[
19
]

The issue on this application is whether the
impugned paragraphs (noted above) are inadmissible, either because they do not
meet the test of relevance or necessity, or because they contain argument.

7.  ANALYSIS

a.
Petition

[
20
]

The petitioner seeks a judicial review of the
Original Decision and the Reconsideration, which confirmed that the Union did
not fail to represent him fairly in dealings with the Employer. The issues raised
by the petition are whether or not the decisions met the standard of review,
and whether or not the petitioner was denied procedural fairness by the LRB. It
is through these live issues that the relevance and necessity of the pleadings and
evidence must be analyzed.

[
21
]

The allegations at para. 59 of the petition,
which deal with the impact of the decisions and conduct of the LRB, Canfor and
the Union on the petitioner, have no relevance in these proceedings. A
consideration of whether the LRB decisions meet the standard of review, and whether
the process in the Original Decision was fair does not create a need to
consider these allegations. In any event, if the LRB fails on either of those
bases it is still not necessary to consider the impact of any such error(s) on
the petitioner because there is no authority by which the Court is able to
award damages on an application for judicial review.
See:
Judicial
Review Procedure Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 241

at
s. 2
; and
McLean
v. British Columbia (Minister of Human Resources)
,
2004 BCSC 285
at
paras.
47-49
.
Accordingly, para. 59 is not relevant or necessary,
contains argument, and should be struck.

[
22
]

Paragraph 60 of the petition alleges that the
actions of Canfor that are at the heart of the complaint were disciplinary. In
the decision under review, the LRB found that the Union acted on its reasonable
belief that the Employer’s actions were non-disciplinary. Evidence regarding
the nature of the Employer’s actions is relevant to the issues in this judicial
review. This paragraph should not be struck from the petition.

[
23
]

At para. 62 (mislabelled paragraph “53” in the
petition), the petitioner alleges that the failure of the Union to meet its
duty of fair representation is consistent with what he describes as misconduct
of Union officials. In support of this position he cites a 2005 internal report
of the Union. This matter, including the internal report of the Union regarding
the alleged misconduct, was put before the LRB’s Reconsideration Panel. The
Union argues that was inappropriate, however I find the allegations set out in
this paragraph may be relevant in determining whether the decision met the
standard of review, and the Union’s application to strike this paragraph should
be denied.

b.
Affidavit

[
24
]

Paragraph 19 of the affidavit contains language
that can be read as argument, but also contains alleged facts that are relevant
to the proceedings. I find that this paragraph can be cured of any defect by
removing the word “incorrectly”. The remainder sets out allegations about what
the petitioner would have done in the prior proceedings had an oral hearing and
full disclosure been granted. This may be of some assistance in determining
whether an oral hearing was required to provide a fair process.

[
25
]

Paragraph 21 of the affidavit is more
problematic than para. 19 in that there is a mixture of argument and fact.
However, there remain important alleged facts among some argumentative
comments. I find any problems with this paragraph can be cured by deleting the
following phrase: “were incorrect, illogical, unreasonable, and unsupported by
the evidence, contrary to the evidence and”. The remainder of the paragraph
concerns the process before the LRB in the prior decision, and in particular
the absence of cross examination, which is relevant to the issue of procedural
fairness.

[
26
]

Paragraph 23 of the affidavit is predominantly
argumentative. Furthermore, it is marked by the type of inflammatory,
adjective-laced language that has no place in an affidavit. For example, it
reads: “conclusions reached... are incorrect, irrational, unreasonable,
unfair...”.  The only option open to this Court to effectively remedy this paragraph
is to strike it in its entirety.

[
27
]

Paragraph 24 of the affidavit is nearly three
pages in length. In it, Mr. Jones takes issue with a number of findings of fact
of the LRB in the various proceedings involving the petitioner. Other evidence that
was before the LRB is emphasized in support of his proposition of unfairness.
Prior to providing the litany of facts that Mr. Jones asserts are the
correct facts, he deposes: “[S]ome of the true facts supported by the material
filed with the LRB include...”. I find this entire paragraph is argument about
the correct inferences to be drawn from the evidence that was before the LRB,
and draws conclusions about that record. If the evidence that supports Mr.
Jones’ position was before the LRB, then it is part of the record before this Court
and can be referred to in argument. This paragraph is unnecessary and
argumentative. Accordingly, it must be struck.

[
28
]

Paragraphs 26 to 28 of the petitioner’s affidavit
allege bias and improper purposes on the part of the Local Executive and
President at the time Mr. Jones’ grievance was being handled. These
allegations were before the LRB and may have some relevance to the question of
whether the decision meets the standard of review. The Union’s application to
strike these paragraphs is denied.

[
29
]

Paragraph 29 of the affidavit includes
allegations about ongoing sexual harassment in the Canfor workplace following
the abandonment of Mr. Jones’ grievance. This has no bearing on the
conduct of the Union with respect to Mr. Jones’ grievance, which is the
issue the LRB addressed. This paragraph has no relevance to the proceedings and
should be struck.

[
30
]

Paragraph 30 of the affidavit refers to the
impact of the investigation by the Employer and the subsequent decisions of the
Employer, the Union, and the LRB respecting Mr. Jones. As discussed above,
these types of facts are not relevant to the issue of whether or not the
decision of the LRB should stand, or whether its process was fair. I find the
application of the Union to strike this paragraph should be granted.

[
31
]

The Union challenges paras. 31 and 32 of the
affidavit on the basis that they contain impermissible argument. While I do not
find that these paragraphs are argument, they do contain allegations about the
impact of Canfor’s decisions and the Union’s response on Mr. Jones and his
reputation at work. None of these factors are relevant to this proceeding.
There is no finding of fact in the decisions of the LRB before me that Mr.
Jones was guilty of sexual harassment, and the personal impact of these
proceedings on Mr. Jones is not relevant. What is relevant before this Court is
evidence that goes to whether the process before the LRB was fair, and the
reasonableness of the decisions resulting from that process. I am unable to
determine how Mr. Jones’ reputation in the workplace has any bearing on those
issues and, accordingly, these paragraphs should be struck from the affidavit.

[
32
]

Finally, para. 33 of the affidavit contains an
allegation that the respondent Union promised to assist the petitioner in his s.
12 complaint under the
Code
and that it failed to do so. What is at
issue before me is the conduct of the Union with respect to the petitioner’s
grievance, not his s. 12 complaint. While I do not accept the Union’s position
with respect to argument, this paragraph is irrelevant and can be struck from
the affidavit on that basis.

8.  CONCLUSION

[
33
]

In summary, I order that:

a)

para. 59 be struck in its entirety from the
petition;

b)

paras. 23-24, 29, and 30-33 be struck in their
entirety from the affidavit;

c)

the word “incorrectly” be struck from para. 19
of the affidavit;

d)

the phrase “were incorrect, illogical,
unreasonable, and unsupported by the evidence, contrary to the evidence and” be
struck from para. 21 of the affidavit; and

e)

except for the two deletions in paras. 19 and 21
of the affidavit, referred to above, the remainder of those paragraphs are
saved.

[
34
]

The Union’s application to strike paras. 60 and
62 (“53”) of the petition is denied, as is the application to strike paras.
26-28 of the affidavit.

[
35
]

As there has been divided success in this
application, I order that, with the exception of the LRB that seeks no order of
costs in relation to the Board, each party shall bear their own costs.

“The Honourable
Madam Justice Maisonville”
